prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Tomb, Place, The

outputs.L1:
Tomb of a millionaire—a multi-millionaire, ladies and gentlemen:  
a place of the dead, where each year they spend  
the usury of twenty-five thousand dollars  
on upkeep and flowers,  
to keep fresh the memory of the dead.

The merchant prince, gone to dust,  
commanded in his written will,  
over the signed name of his last testament,  
that twenty-five thousand dollars be set aside  
for roses, lilacs, hydrangeas, and tulips;  
for perfume and color,  
for the sweetness of remembrance  
around his last long home.

(A hundred cash girls want nickels  
to go to the movies tonight.  
In the back stalls of a hundred saloons,  
women sit at tables,  
drinking with men  
or waiting for men  
with loose silver dollars jingling in their pockets.  
In a hundred furnished rooms  
there is a girl who sells silk,  
or dress goods,  
or leather goods,  
for six dollars a week in wages;  
and when she pulls on her stockings in the morning,  
she is reckless about God,  
and the newspapers,  
and the police,  
and the talk of her hometown,  
or the name people call her.)
outputs.L2:
A wealthy man’s grave—indeed, the burial place of a man worth many millions, ladies and gentlemen.  
This house of the dead receives, year after year, the interest from twenty-five thousand dollars,  
money reserved for maintenance and blossoms,  
so that the memory of the man buried there may be kept vivid and adorned.

This lord of commerce, now reduced to dust,  
ordered in his will, beneath the signature of his final legal testament,  
that twenty-five thousand dollars should be put away  
for roses, lilacs, hydrangeas, and tulips—  
for fragrance, color, and the tender sweetness of being remembered  
around the place where he will rest forever.

Meanwhile, a hundred shop girls need five-cent pieces tonight so they can go to the movies.  
In the rear rooms of a hundred saloons, women sit at tables,  
drinking with men or waiting for men who carry loose silver dollars rattling in their pockets.  
And in a hundred rented rooms, there is a girl selling silk, dress goods, or leather goods for six dollars a week;  
when she puts on her stockings in the morning, she no longer cares much about God, the newspapers, the police,  
what people in her hometown say, or the name others give her.
outputs.L3:
A millionaire’s tomb is maintained each year with an astonishing sum of twenty-five thousand dollars, set aside solely for its upkeep and for the flowers that surround it. Even after death, the wealthy merchant is protected by money, beauty, and careful attention. His grave is not left to decay or be forgotten; instead, it is preserved as a place of luxury and display.

According to the dead merchant’s will, roses, lilacs, hydrangeas, and tulips are to bloom in his memory. These flowers are meant to keep his name alive through color, fragrance, and beauty. The tomb becomes a symbol of wealth continuing beyond the grave, as if money can purchase remembrance and dignity even after life has ended.

The poem sharply contrasts this lavish care for the dead man’s resting place with the hardship endured by working women. Cash girls and low-paid saleswomen live with little comfort and few opportunities for happiness. They struggle to afford small pleasures, basic survival, and a sense of dignity in a world that demands their labor but gives them very little in return.

Through this contrast, the text criticizes a society with distorted values. It shows how enormous sums can be spent on honoring a rich man after his death, while living women who work hard every day are neglected and underpaid. The flowers on the millionaire’s grave become more than decorations; they represent the injustice of a world that beautifies death for the wealthy while ignoring the suffering of the poor.
outputs.L4:
A millionaire dies, and in his will he carefully provides for the preservation of his memory. Not merely a modest marker or a simple resting place, but a lavish tomb is to stand as a monument to his wealth and importance. To ensure that the place remains beautiful and impressive, he sets aside $25,000 a year for flowers, decoration, and upkeep. Long after his life has ended, fresh blossoms are to be placed around his grave, attendants are to care for the grounds, and the public is to be reminded that a rich man once lived and expected to be remembered.

The spectacle is meant to inspire admiration, but it instead exposes a deep moral contradiction. Thousands of dollars are devoted each year to honoring a man who can no longer see, smell, or enjoy the flowers placed upon his tomb. The money serves no living hunger, heals no suffering, and relieves no human burden. It is spent to preserve vanity after death, to keep alive the name of one who possessed more than enough in life and still demanded tribute in the grave.

This extravagance becomes even more troubling when set beside the lives of working women who struggle daily for survival. In factories, shops, laundries, and offices, women labor long hours for wages barely sufficient to pay for food, rent, clothing, and shelter. Many are underpaid, overworked, and treated as though their needs are insignificant. They give their strength and health to produce comfort and wealth for others, yet they often remain trapped in poverty. A fraction of the money reserved for flowers on a dead man’s tomb could provide meals, medical care, education, rest, or decent living conditions for women who are very much alive.

The contrast is harsh and revealing. Society finds a way to protect the dignity of the rich even after death, but it often fails to protect the dignity of the poor while they live. A grave may be surrounded by roses, while living women go without bread. Marble may be polished and lawns carefully trimmed, while workers’ bodies are worn down by exhausting labor. The dead millionaire is guaranteed perpetual care, while the living laborer must fight for the smallest measure of security.

Such a memorial is therefore not simply a private expression of grief or remembrance. It becomes a symbol of injustice. It shows how wealth can be used to glorify itself rather than to serve humanity. The issue is not that the dead should be forgotten, but that the living should not be neglected. Memory purchased at such a price becomes offensive when human need is ignored. A society that spends fortunes decorating tombs while workers lack the necessities of life has confused values: it honors wealth more than labor, reputation more than compassion, and the dead more than the living.

The true measure of a person’s legacy should not be the cost of the flowers placed upon his grave, but the good he has done for those who remain. Money used to ease suffering, improve working conditions, educate children, or give struggling women a chance at a decent life would create a far more meaningful memorial than any monument of stone. A tomb may preserve a name, but justice and generosity preserve a life’s worth. In this contrast between a millionaire’s costly grave and the poverty of working women, the moral imbalance of society is laid bare.
outputs.L5:
**The Tomb and the Place**

The tomb stood in a quiet place beyond the village, where the wind moved softly through the grass and the trees leaned over the path like silent guardians. No one knew exactly how old it was, but everyone spoke of it with respect. It was not just a tomb; it was a place of memory.

People came there to think, to grieve, and sometimes to find peace. The stones were worn by time, yet they seemed to hold stories of those who had lived before. In that still place, the past felt close, as if the world had paused for a moment.

The tomb reminded everyone that every life leaves a mark. Even when voices fade and names are forgotten, places can remember.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the style of Carl Sandburg contrasting a wealthy man's lavish tomb maintenance with the poverty of working-class women in the city.
counterfactuals.output:
The rich man is dead  
and the marble knows his name.

Every morning a hired hand  
wipes the rain off his angel,  
clips the grass around his sleep,  
sets fresh lilies in a bronze cup  
where no mouth will smell them.

There is a little house for his bones  
with a door of iron vines,  
with windows nobody looks through,  
with stone steps washed cleaner  
than the hands of the women  
who scrub downtown floors at night.

They come out at dawn  
from offices shining like ice,  
their backs bent under pails,  
their shoes split,  
their fingers red from lye and winter.

They pass the bakeries  
breathing warm bread into the street  
and count nickels in their gloves.

One has a cough.  
One has a baby asleep in a room  
where the plaster falls like old snow.  
One has a husband gone to the yards,  
or gone nowhere,  
or gone into the bottle and the dark.

The rich man’s grave has roses.  
The women have onions, coal dust,  
rent due Friday,  
and a landlord with a hard mouth.

At noon the caretaker polishes the name again.  
Gold letters.  
A good man, the stone says.  
Beloved.  
Honored.  
At rest.

The city clatters on its iron feet.

Under the elevated,  
a woman opens her dinner pail  
and finds two crusts,  
a boiled potato,  
a silence she has carried all morning.

The rich man sleeps  
under acres of trimmed green.

The women lie down late  
in rooms where the wind comes in,  
and rise before the sun  
to wash the floors of men  
who will someday buy  
clean marble  
and flowers  
and a man to keep the weeds away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a socially critical modernist poem about a millionaire who leaves $25,000 a year for flowers on his grave while poor shop girls struggle to survive.
counterfactuals.output:
**Legacy with Cut Flowers**

In the financial district  
a bronze door keeps his name polished.  
In the cemetery  
his marble drinks the weather.

He has arranged it:

twenty-five thousand dollars a year  
for lilies, roses, hot-house orchids—  
a white procession  
to expire beautifully  
above his bones.

The florist signs the invoice.  
The banker nods.  
The grass is clipped into obedience.

Meanwhile, at five o’clock,  
the shop girls spill from the lit windows,  
thin coats buttoned against March,  
hands raw from ribbon, paper, coin,  
their wages folded small  
as bus transfers.

They have stood all day  
selling silk to women  
who do not ask the price,  
smiling until the smile  
ached like a second spine.

At night they count:  
rent, bread, stockings, coal—  
subtracting hunger  
with a pencil stub.

One takes the long way home  
past the cemetery wall.  
Over it, she can smell the flowers.

So much sweetness  
for a man who cannot breathe.

So much color  
for eyes that have become stone.

The city calls this order.  
The will calls it devotion.  
The newspaper calls it a curious bequest.

But the girls know  
what money is  
when it is not marble:

a room with heat,  
milk in the morning,  
a tooth saved,  
a winter coat,  
one hour sitting down  
without being watched.

Under the earth  
the millionaire receives  
his annual spring.

Above the earth  
the living wilt.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem that sounds like early 20th-century American free verse, with stark imagery of wealth, death, usury, saloons, cash girls, and furnished rooms.
counterfactuals.output:
In the city of brass spittoons and winter windows  
the money slept upstairs,  
warm in its ledgers,  
buttoned into vaults like a dead man in black cloth.

Below, the saloons opened their yellow mouths.  
Men went in with wages folded small as prayers  
and came out emptied,  
their shadows longer than their names.

The usurer sat under a green lamp,  
a little moon of bile,  
counting the ribs of the poor  
through their coats.  
His fingers were white worms  
traveling over paper.

O cash girls—thin birds behind counters—  
running with change in your hands,  
your feet quick on the worn floors,  
your eyes already old from seeing  
silk go upward,  
hunger go down.

At night the furnished rooms received us:  
iron bed, cracked pitcher,  
one chair lame at the leg,  
wallpaper blooming with damp like a disease.  
A gas flame trembled  
as if it knew the price of breath.

Somewhere a rich man died softly  
among curtains and physicians.  
Somewhere a poor man died loudly  
on a stair,  
with rent due,  
and no one wrote the hour correctly.

The city kept its accounts.  
It charged for bread,  
for sleep,  
for the hand laid briefly on another hand.  
It charged the dead for their boxes  
and the living for standing beside them.

Yet morning came up gray over the roofs,  
and the milk wagons rattled like bones,  
and girls with red wrists hurried to work  
through streets washed clean of nothing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a satirical elegy for a dead merchant prince whose will funds roses and tulips for his tomb, juxtaposed with underpaid women seeking nickels for the movies.
counterfactuals.output:
**Elegy for a Merchant Prince**

Here lies the Prince of Wholesale Lace,  
Departed from the market-place;  
His ledgers closed, his shutters drawn,  
His final bargain neatly gone.

He left, with admirable gloom,  
Ten thousand dollars to his tomb—  
For roses, monthly, fresh and red,  
And tulips nodding at his head.

Let no harsh weed presume to grow  
Where gilt initials sleep below;  
Let gardeners, paid on proper terms,  
Defend his dust from civic worms.

Meanwhile, outside the cemetery gate,  
The women punch the clock till late,  
Hem collars, stitch, and cough, and freeze,  
For wages trimmed by his trustees.

They count their coins with reddened thumbs,  
As evening through the factory hums;  
A nickel short, they laugh and plead—  
One picture show is all they need.

O generous bones! O scented stone!  
How sweet the blooms you call your own,  
While living hands, in winter air,  
Go flowerless home from making wear.

Sleep well, great lord of thread and rent,  
Your will is law, your cash well spent;  
The roses bow, the tulips flare,  
And no one asks how they got there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a gritty urban poem beginning with “Tomb of a millionaire” and ending with a parenthetical passage about shop girls, saloons, wages, newspapers, police, and reputation.
counterfactuals.output:
Tomb of a millionaire,  
marble sweating under soot,  
your angels cough black dust  
while the avenue gnaws its cigar  
and spits sparks into the gutter.

Down where the elevated train  
shakes the teeth in a beggar’s grin,  
men carry lunch pails like empty verdicts,  
women stitch daylight into coats  
they will never wear.

The river drags its oily back  
past warehouses and locked doors,  
past boys with switchblades of hunger  
and mothers counting pennies  
as if prayer came in copper.

At midnight the city opens  
its one red eye—  
neon trembling on rain,  
boots in alleys,  
sirens braiding the dark  
with a hard blue thread.

And above it all,  
your stone name sleeps,  
fat with silence,  
while the living scrape and bargain  
for a room, a crust, a little heat,  
a morning that doesn’t arrive armed.

The pigeons know.  
The rats know.  
The ash barrels overflow  
with yesterday’s promises,  
and the wind goes door to door  
collecting what the rich forgot to bury.

(shop girls with tired feet, saloons with yellow windows, wages thin as smoke, newspapers shouting murder and miracles, police pacing the corners, reputation hanging by a thread)
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
